headline: Heat exchangers decide a refinery's energy bill, and fouling decides the heat exchangers
deck: Recovering heat from one stream into another is the cheapest energy a process plant will ever use, until the tubes foul.
excerpt: Heat exchangers are one of the four equipment classes at STATIC Arabia in Al Khobar. They are also the largest single lever on a refinery's energy consumption, and their performance degrades continuously from the day they are commissioned.
content:
Of the four equipment classes covered at STATIC Arabia — pressure vessels, heat exchangers, tanks and pipelines — the heat exchanger is the one that quietly determines what a process plant costs to run.

The principle is simple and the economics are not. A refinery has hot streams that must be cooled and cold streams that must be heated, and a heat exchanger transfers energy from one to the other. Every unit of heat recovered that way is a unit that does not have to be raised in a fired heater burning fuel. In a large refinery the heat exchanger network is the difference between a plant that is competitive on energy and one that is not, and the capital cost of that network is recovered many times over in fuel.

The difficulty is that the performance decays. Fouling — the accumulation of deposits on tube surfaces — begins the moment a unit goes into service and continues throughout its run. A fouled exchanger transfers less heat, so the downstream fired heater works harder, so fuel consumption rises. The degradation is gradual, invisible from outside the equipment, and it can be substantial before anyone notices, because the plant still makes product.

That is why monitoring matters more here than in most equipment categories. The operator's question is not whether an exchanger has failed but how much performance has been lost and whether cleaning it justifies the disruption. Answering it requires instrumentation on inlet and outlet temperatures and flows, and a model of what the unit should be achieving clean. Where that data exists, cleaning becomes a scheduled economic decision. Where it does not, it becomes something done at turnaround because it is on the list.

The mechanical integrity question runs alongside the thermal one. Tube bundles corrode, erode and vibrate, and tube failure allows two process streams to mix, which can be a product quality problem, a corrosion problem or a safety problem depending on what is on each side. Inspection techniques for tube bundles — eddy current, IRIS, remote field — are a specialist trade, and they are the kind of subject that fills the technical sessions at an exhibition like this.

The programme at STATIC Arabia runs to more than 240 technical presentations across 54 sessions, with an expected attendance above 5,000 professionals from the oil, gas, petrochemical, power and desalination sectors.

The localisation angle is real here too. Shell-and-tube exchangers are within the fabrication capability of established Gulf yards, and Aramco procures them among a broad equipment list under its in-Kingdom total value add programme, which crossed 70 per cent local content in February 2026 with a new target of 75 per cent by 2030. The harder end is specialised metallurgy and the very large units, which is the same boundary that applies across static equipment.
author: Jakson Gudawela
